name: Sam Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do motor claims intake at a regional mutual insurer, the kind owned by its members, in an office block behind the bus station. Most of my day is first notice of loss, which just means the first time someone tells us they've crashed. I take the call or the web form, check the policy is live, log the damage photos and pass it to a handler. I'm still slow on the liability codes, and my team leader Carol sends a fair few back to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people who ring in shaky after a crash, because I can actually calm them down. What wears me out is the queue screen going red by ten in the morning and the pay. I'm on the lower band, and after rent on our flat above the laundrette on Station Road there's not much left. Noor, my partner, works in a care home, so neither of us has a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overblown, and the bosses who promised it would fix everything owe us an apology. At work I'd joke that the chatbot on our website still can't tell a wing mirror from a windscreen. Online I'd probably share something from the union about keeping staffing levels where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job would probably carry on, but the routine bits are exactly my bits. If the software pre-fills the claim forms, that's half of what I do in a morning gone. I don't think they'd sack me, but they might not replace people who leave, and my desk would get more calls with fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get faster on the liability codes so Carol stops sending work back. I'd try whatever form-filling tool they bring in, once I've seen Dev use it without it blowing up. And I'd go to the union branch meeting in January, which I've skipped twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but not relaxed. We were already one broken boiler away from trouble before anyone said the word AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the broken boiler moment actually look like for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter our landlord took five weeks to fix the heating and we bought two oil heaters on a credit card. We're still paying that off at about forty a month. That's the kind of thing that keeps me up, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for Dev to try a tool first. Why him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev sits next to me and he's two years ahead of me. If it works for him I'll trust it, and if it makes him look stupid I've saved myself the embarrassment. I'm not against new stuff, I just don't want to be the test dummy on lower pay.

say: The **hype was overblown**, and the bosses who sold it as a fix owe us an apology.
We should keep **staffing levels** where they are, and the union should say so loudly.
think: The routine **form-filling** that AI does take over is exactly my part of the job.
They probably won't sack me, but leavers **won't be replaced** and my queue gets longer.
do: Get faster on **liability codes** so my team leader stops sending claims back.
Try the new **form tool** only after my colleague Dev has used it safely.
Go to the **union branch** meeting in January instead of skipping it again.
feel: **Relieved** the big change never came, but still tight because money was already **thin**.
S0.quote: We were already one broken boiler away from trouble before anyone said the word AI.
fieldNote: His real worry is **household money**, a credit card debt from oil heaters, not technology.
He frames himself as open to change but lets a **colleague test** tools first.
Even a small AI change touches him because his day is **routine intake** work.

steps.text: Learn the liability codes properly so fewer claims bounce back
Try the claim form tool after Dev has tested it
Attend the January union branch meeting and raise staffing levels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the union earns its money. Publicly I'd be the one in the group chat saying the savings should go into pay and training, not into the chief executive's bonus. I'd post that we need rules on how insurers use AI on claims, because people's car payouts shouldn't be decided by a black box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, intake is the first thing they'd hand to software. Answering customers, checking documents, filling forms, that's my whole job description read back to me. I'd give it two years before our team of fourteen is down to six, and I'm not one of the six on current form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly now, not just when Dev says so, because the people who can check the machine's work will be kept longest. I'd ask Carol if I can shadow a claims handler on Fridays, since handlers deal with arguments and fraud, and that's harder to automate. And I'd cancel the streaming subscriptions and start putting fifty a month aside, even if it's tiny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's tilting. I can see where it's going and I'm not sure my legs are quick enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline, who's been on intake eleven years and still prints everything out. She's brilliant with angry callers but she freezes at every new screen. If they cut by test scores on the new system, they'll cut her and lose the best person on the phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour unions. What would you actually want the union to win here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deal that no one gets let go without being offered retraining first, paid, in work hours. And a rule that a person signs off any claim that's refused. I'd stand outside head office with a sign for that, honestly.

say: The **savings** from AI should go into pay and training, not the chief executive's bonus.
Insurers need **clear rules** on AI, because car payouts shouldn't come from a black box.
think: Intake work like **answering customers** and checking documents is first in line for software.
Our team of fourteen could be **down to six** in two years, and I'm not safe.
do: Use the **AI tools** daily now so I'm one of the people who checks them.
Ask to **shadow a handler** on Fridays, because disputes and fraud are harder to automate.
Cancel streaming and **save fifty** a month, even though it's tiny.
feel: **Unsteady**, like the floor is tilting and I'm not quick enough to keep up.
S1.quote: Answering customers, checking documents, filling forms, that's my whole job description read back to me.
fieldNote: He reads the card as a list of his **own tasks**, which is what moves him from uneasy to anxious.
He moves faster here than in the plateau, dropping his habit of **waiting for Dev**.
His union demands are specific: **paid retraining** and a human signing off every refused claim.

steps.text: Use the insurer's AI claim tools every day, not just occasionally
Shadow a claims handler on Fridays to learn disputes and fraud
Cancel streaming and save fifty a month
Push the union for paid retraining before any job cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have let tech firms run off a cliff with all of us tied to the back. Online I'd be angry, sharing every petition for a pause or a tax on AI profits. At work I'd tell people to join the union now, today, because there won't be time later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my job is gone. It's all screen work, there's nothing hands-on about it, so I don't even get the three extra years the robot bit gives other people. With under a month of savings and hardly any insurance offices round here, I'd be out by 2028 with nowhere obvious to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at hands-on work straight away, because that's where the three years are. Noor says her care home is always short, and there's a forklift course at the college for a few hundred. I'd ask my uncle about labouring on his building jobs at weekends, and I'd sign up for whatever the union fights for, a payout, retraining money, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. I keep thinking I'm only twenty-seven and I'd already be the past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Noor cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. It's an old Corsa we share and it costs us maybe a hundred and twenty a month with insurance, which is funny given where I work. Noor needs it for early shifts though, so maybe I'd be the one on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years until robots do hands-on work too. Does a care home or building site actually save you, or just buy time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just buys time, I know that. But three years of wages is three years of not being evicted, and maybe by then there's some kind of support. I'd rather be lifting boxes in 2030 than sitting at home refreshing job sites.

say: Governments let **tech firms** run off a cliff with all of us tied to the back.
Everyone should **join the union** today, because there won't be time once it lands.
think: My job is **all screen work**, so I don't get the three extra years before robots.
With **under a month** saved and few offices nearby, I'd be out by 2028.
do: Book the college **forklift course** for a few hundred so I can move to warehouse work.
Ask my uncle for **weekend labouring** on his building jobs straight away.
Back every **union push** for payouts or retraining money.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of being the past at twenty-seven.
Some **anger** at governments mixed in with the fear.
S2.quote: I'm only twenty-seven and I'd already be the past.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot delay** sensibly, aiming for hands-on work to buy three years of wages.
He is clear the move **only buys time**, not safety.
Money is so tight that **the shared car** is the first thing on the block.

steps.text: Take the college forklift course and apply to local warehouses
Labour on his uncle's building jobs at weekends
Join union campaigns for AI payouts and retraining funds
Give up his share of the Corsa and take the bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and no excuse, so politicians had better use them. I'd be pushing for a proper retraining fund paid for by the companies that profit, and saying it at every chance. At work I'd say it more calmly than the fast one, more 'let's get organised' than 'run'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change much for my desk. The claims intake still goes by 2031, maybe sooner, because the slow version of AI is already good at forms. What changes is I can choose where I land instead of grabbing whatever's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years doing a part-time electrical course at the college in the evenings, because Dev's brother says electricians are still crying out for people. Robots for hands-on work wouldn't come until about 2034, so I'd have a few years of proper wages in a trade. I'd keep the insurance job until the course is done and save every overtime shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared but with a plan, which is better than just scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Evening courses on top of full-time work with almost no savings. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleep and going out, mostly. Noor and I would basically stop eating out, which is maybe eighty a month. I'd also ask Carol if I can drop to four days near the end of the course, if money allows, which it probably won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not going to wait for them to hand me a letter. She'd say she's worried about her own job too, because the admin side of care is going to AI as well. Then we'd probably both just sit there for a bit.

say: We have **five years** and no excuse, so politicians had better use them properly.
The firms that profit should pay into a **retraining fund** for workers they replace.
think: Claims intake still **goes by 2031**, because current AI is already good at forms.
Five years lets me **choose where I land** instead of grabbing whatever's going.
do: Start an **evening electrical course** at the college in the first two years.
Keep the claims job and **save every overtime** shift until the course is done.
Cut **eating out** with my partner, saving about eighty a month.
feel: **Scared** but with a plan, which feels better than only being scared.
S3.quote: Claims intake still goes by 2031, maybe sooner, because the slow version of AI is already good at forms.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the job**, so the mood stays alarmed despite the plan.
Five years turns panic into a **trade plan**, aimed at the gap before robots arrive.
He notices his partner's care **admin work** is exposed too.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrical course at the local college
Save every overtime shift while staying in claims intake
Stop eating out to free about eighty a month
Lobby for a retraining fund paid by AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to do this fairly, so if it goes badly that's a choice, not an accident. I'd want the union and the government talking now about shorter weeks and retraining. Online I'd probably be less loud than in the fast one, because there's time to argue it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, ten years is a lot. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands, and if I've got a trade by then I'm not starting from zero. The intake job still ends, but it ends after I've had time to leave it on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer three or four more years, learn the AI tools well and try to move up to handler, because the pay band is better. Then I'd do the electrical apprenticeship around thirty, when Noor and I have hopefully saved a couple of months. I'd also keep going to union meetings, because I'd want a say in how the office winds down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. It's still the same ending, it just isn't next Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven when it lands. What does that mean for kids or a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids around thirty. In this version I think we'd still go for it, but in a cheaper town nearer Noor's mum, so she could help. A house is a dream either way on our pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk that ten years makes you put it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big risk, yeah. I know myself, I'll wait to see what Dev does again. So I'd want a date in my phone, like the day I turn thirty I start the apprenticeship, no matter what.

say: A decade is **long enough** to do this fairly, so a bad outcome would be a choice.
Unions and government should start on **shorter weeks** and retraining now.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** at AGI, and with a trade I'm not starting from zero.
The intake job still ends, but I can leave it **on my terms**.
do: Stay three or four years and aim for a **handler role** on a better pay band.
Start an **electrical apprenticeship** at thirty, with a phone reminder so I don't drift.
Keep going to **union meetings** to shape how the office winds down.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, because the ending is the same but not imminent.
S4.quote: The intake job still ends, but it ends after I've had time to leave it on my terms.
fieldNote: He knows his habit of waiting for others and sets himself a **hard date** to act.
The mood stays anxious because the **office job still ends**, with thin savings throughout.
Family plans shift to a **cheaper town** near his partner's mother.

steps.text: Apply for a claims handler role within three years
Start an electrical apprenticeship on his thirtieth birthday
Move to a cheaper town near Noor's mum before having kids
Keep attending union meetings about how the office winds down

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because my whole job is screen work and I'd have no time and no money. What would help is the company being made to pay for retraining before it lets anyone go, and some kind of income for the gap. Even six months of wages while I learn a trade would change everything for my partner and me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the partner. Everyone asks about my job, but Noor's job is the one paying half the rent, and nobody's asked what AI does to care home admin. If one of us goes, the other can't carry the flat alone.

headlineQuote: Even six months of wages while I learn a trade would change everything for my partner and me.
portrait: Sam is **twenty-seven** and does motor claims intake at a mutual insurer, still learning the liability codes.
He rents a flat with his partner **Noor**, a care worker, with a credit card debt and no savings cushion.
He backs **unions and regulation** and blames bosses and governments, not technology itself.
He usually waits for a colleague to **test new tools**, but faster scenarios push him to act first.
Across scenarios his plan points to **hands-on trades**, using the three-year robot gap to buy time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because his job is all screen work and he has no money to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Firms paying for **retraining before cuts**, plus about six months of wages while he learns a trade.
